speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of lhe Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to associate myself and the members of the party to which I belong with this tribute of respect to the memory of a very gallant member of this house. I use the word "gallant" advisedly, because it is well known to all hon. members that he suffered greatly during the last year and a half or more, and his illness was such as to call for a high degree of courage. His presence in this house in itself was a manifestation of that courage.
I did not have the privilege of knowing Mr. Hartt for the number of years that he was known to many other hon. members, but I do know that his industry and the stand he took on public affairs had won the regard and the admiration of members in all parts of the house. It perhaps was both natural and fitting that a man who came originally from a country which has suffered so much under the tyranny of communism should have identified himself so vigorously with a campaign against communism in this country.
In his passing this house has lost a man who, whatever other grounds of difference there might be in political opinion, certainly represented the common viewpoint in regard to the preservation of our system of democracy and the traditional institutions which we wish to preserve.

Mr. Speaker, in remembering the late Mr. Hartt I think it is a tribute both to his ability and to the opportunities provided by this country that, having come from Roumania, he should have achieved the distinction of membership in the legislature of Quebec and in this parliament.
As occasionally I sat here listening to him I admired his ability to use both the English and the French language, as well as, of course, his mother tongue and I believe related languages. We wish to join with all others in the house in expressing sympathy to his widow and his sons in their bereavement.

Mr. Speaker, it is a cause for deepest regret that a man should be taken from our, midst at the early age of fifty-four. At that age a man

The late Mr. Maurice Hartt has acquired just enough knowledge and wisdom to be of real value to any body of legislators with which he might be connected.
Mr. Hartt proved himself to be very sincere, a man of great courage, as was pointed out, and a man disposed to face facts as they are. These things I believe constitute a great tribute to his memory.
This group desires to join with those who have already spoken in expressing our deep sympathy with the bereaved ones, and our appreciation of a fellow member who has gone.

Mr. Speaker,
I speak from a sense of personal loss. I knew Maurice Hartt, having first met him twenty-five years ago when he came to the counties of Essex and Kent to speak on behalf of an old friend of mine, Eddie Odette, who was running in the constituency. I remember on that occasion hearing him speak at Tilbury and Belle River, and speaking in most fluent French. Then, as in later years, he was a most forceful speaker.
Our paths did not cross often. However, we met again in Ottawa in 1947, when he recaptured Cartier for Canadians. On account of ill health he seldom spoke in the house, but he did make some fiery and worth-while contributions to the cause which was closest to his heart-establishment and recognition of the state of Israel.
He was a man of intense loyalties-loyalty to his country, loyalty to his party, loyalty to his religion; and he was fiercely loyal to his friends. His great interest in life was the people in his riding of Cartier. There were many underprivileged people there who made many demands upon him. He met those demands as well as any member could have met them.
It is interesting to note the statistics in Cartier. That riding has a very high member-mortality rate. Public service had shared much of Mr. Hartt's life. In 1939 he was a member of the legislature of Quebec. He came to this house in 1947, but he took up community life in the city of Montreal from the time he graduated from Queen's and moved to Montreal.
To the public lifd of this country he gave a mind that was keen and thoughtful and a heart that was kind and considerate. He was a man who loved a fight, giving as he got. As recently as Monday of this week I received a cheerful and buoyant letter from him telling me of plans he had in mind for the future. Hon. members will appreciate what a shock it was to me when yesterday afternoon I was informed he had passed on.


I saw him a few times during his illness. From our conversations I feel sure he would want me to say what I am now going to say. I wish particularly to thank the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), you, Mr. Speaker, and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), for their thoughtfulness and kindness to Mr. Hartt during his long illness.
May I join with hon. members in extending deepest sympathy to his wife and children. He leaves to them a cherished memory of a very high reputation earned in the service of his country.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure I would be remiss in my duty if I failed to join in paying tribute to the memory of the late member for Cartier, who was my roommate for some considerable time.
I, too, wish to express my sympathy to Mrs. Hartt and her two sons. It is tragic to learn that at the early age of fifty-four years a man of Mr. Hartt's calibre should have been called. As his former roommate I had the opportunity for many discussions with him about the hard knocks one sometimes gets in life. I am sure those who have known him will miss his pleasant smile.

POLYMER CORPORATION, SARNIA    REPORT AS TO THREATENED STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Yesterday, in view of the threatened strike at the Polymer Corporation, because of representations made to me I asked the following question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe):
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It is based on a dispatch in today's Globe and Mail, and also on a telegram which I have just received. The dispatch indicates a threatened strike of employees of Polymer Corporation which would involve all the major industries in Sarnia. Is the Minister of Trade and Commerce prepared at this time to make a statement to the house?
I asked the question because it affected not only the major industries in the city of Sarnia, but also those in western Ontario, inasmuch as the plant supplies electricity to the extent of about 40,000 horsepower. This was the answer given at that time by the Minister of Trade and Commerce:
Mr. Speaker, I have had no report today from the Polymer Corporation, but a few days ago it was reported to me that a conciliation board had been sitting on a labour-management dispute, and that the board had brought in a unanimous finding which the management intended to accept. What has developed since I cannot say. The management of the corporation handle their own labour negotiations. From what I know of the relations between

the management and labour at Polymer I can assure my hon. friend that there is not likely to be a strike.
My interpretation of the minister's answer was-except for the last few words which are so important-that there would be no strike. Having received the minister's answer, I wired the union at Sarnia accordingly. My interpretation of what the minister said was borne out by a press report in the Globe and Mail of today's issue, which states:
Trade Minister Howe said today he could assure the Commons that there will be no strike at the government-owned Polymer rubber corporation at Sarnia.
I understand that the only other morning paper in western Ontario, the London Free Press, carries the same interpretation of the reply given by the minister.
Inasmuch as there is a vast difference between "there will be no strike" and "there is not likely to be a strike", I wonder if in view of the seriousness of the situation, in case there should be a strike, the minister would clarify the record.

maintopic: DR. LEOPOLD INFELD KNOWLEDGE OF ATOMIC ENERGY    PLANS TO TEACH IN WARSAW

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: DR. LEOPOLD INFELD KNOWLEDGE OF ATOMIC ENERGY    PLANS TO TEACH IN WARSAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer to a matter, not by way of a question but under the general provision as to matters of public interest. It is one that I think should be brought immediately to the attention of the government, in view of the possible implications. It is also a matter that should be of common concern to the whole house.
In the issue of The Ensign dated March 18 there is a statement on page 3 headed: "Einstein aide plans to teach in Warsaw." The subheading is:	"Communist Poland
recalls Toronto Varsity scientist." In the article there is the statement that Dr. Leopold Infeld, who is a teacher of mathematics at the university of Toronto, has announced that he is to proceed to Warsaw to teach in the universities there, and to make plans for certain educational programs in cooperation with the government of Poland. The article further discloses the fact that, and I quote:
. . . he is thoroughly familiar with the theory and much of the practical application of atomic energy.
It is also stated here-and I have other evidence to the same effect-that in 1946 he
Inquiries of the Ministry predicted that Russia would have the atomic bomb within three years. It was a strangely accurate prediction. It also is disclosed-and this does surprise me-that this scientist, who was a refugee from Poland and was welcomed as a professor at the university of Toronto, was teaching in Warsaw and Krakow last summer.
I think all of us are fully aware that in the communist states education is something that conforms to more than academic standards. Those who are engaged as teachers in their universities are certainly under certain limitations and are subject to qualifications that do not relate to their academic standing alone. I bring this matter before the house because I think it will be a most remarkable thing if it is true that Dr. Infeld is going to apply to the university of Toronto for a sabbatical year-not just the summer-during which he will receive half pay from Canada's largest university while he is in Poland for the purpose of organizing educational activities under the guidance of a communist government. His statement is significant in view of the words in quotation marks in the article, which is in turn a quotation from the Toronto Globe and Mail, that Dr. Infeld said some time ago he would return to Poland when "a progressive government in a new Poland that needs him would attract him back to Europe."
That statement is not open to much doubt if the words are correctly attributed to Dr. Infeld. I believe that the appropriate department of the government should look into the matter immediately; and, having regard to what has already happened under not dissimi-'ir circumstances, appropriate steps should be taken to ascertain the circumstances under which Dr. Infeld plans to return to Poland armed with certain atomic knowledge that he gained during two years' association with Dr. Einstein in the United States, and from several years' activity in the fields of mathematics and physics at the university of Toronto.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am hoping that during the time I shall occupy the floor of the house today I shall be able to have the ear of members of the Progressive Conservative party and as

The Address-Mr. Low many as possible of the members of the Liberal party, particularly those who are attending their first or second session. I refer to the newcomers on the Liberal side of the house, because I know that many of them have not had much opportunity to study the proposals that have been put forward from time to time by the Social Credit party in the house. It is because I should like to have them know exactly what we think about some of the important matters facing the Canadian people today that I appeal to them to listen. Furthermore, I appeal both to the Progressive Conservatives and to the Liberals to take seriously what I am going to say today, and then to take part in the debate and show cause why the things I say are not correct, if they think they are not.
I challenge them to take up the arguments that I shall present and debate them. Let them come to grips with them rather than try to brush them off by simply saying that it is all idealism, foolhardiness, or something of the kind.
Before I proceed, Mr. Speaker, may I ask you to call hon. members to order, because no one can hear as long as the buzzing which is going on at the present moment continues.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I first appeal to the Progressive Conservative party.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is your first mistake.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
We shall see whether it is a mistake. I believe in appealing to the reason of any man, no matter what he calls himself. After all, the names of the parties are merely labels, and frankly I have failed to find very much difference between that side of the house and my colleagues to the right, except that the group on the other side of the house seems more concerned about getting elected than doing something for the people.
I want to direct these views to the Progressive Conservative party, because the matter before us today is the amendment that has been moved by that party.
I should like to go back just a few years and remind them of some of the things said by a great leader of their party. I refer to the former prime minister of this country, Mr. R. B. Bennett. I am quoting now from a radio speech he made on January 4, 1935, I presume during the course of the election campaign, or at least leading up to that campaign. This speech is recorded in a little blue booklet called "The Premier Speaks to the People." I was attracted by some things the former prime minister had to say to the country over the radio that evening. I quote:
My friends, when many of us talk about unemployment, we fail to realize what unemployment
rMr. Low.]

means. Unemployment is the visible expression of those inherent defects in the capitalist system which I have deen discussing.
I have said I would end unemployment. That is why I have said and say again I will reform the system. The cynic may deride my determined effort to do so, but those of faith and sincere purpose will support me to the end of the road.
That was spoken as though from deep conviction that there were faults and weaknesses in the capitalist system which had to be corrected if we were to get at the root of our troubles and solve the unemployment problem. From Mr. Bennett's statement it is apparent that he was not trying to treat symptoms but rather was acknowledging the fact that we were producing to a far greater extent than the Canadian people were allowed to consume, and that the result of that fault was unemployment. Mr. Bennett declared at that time that he would reform the system. I could quote other statements he made during the same series of broadcasts. One that came over the radio on January 9, 1935, contained this statement:
In my three previous talks I have declared definitely and repeatedly that there must be reform of our capitalist system and that the time for that reform has come. I have shown you that until the worst of the depression was over, reform was not possible. I have told you what we have done by other means to carry the country through the depression. I have said that further progress without reform is improbable.
There were a number of other addresses; and by the way I hold in my hand one of those addresses that has a foreword by an hon. member who now sits on the other side of the house, who at that time was a great hockey player and sportsman-the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Conacher)-supporting the then prime minister of Canada, Mr. Bennett, and declaring to the country that the Conservatives were the reform party, not the Liberals.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That was before I grew up, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
What I have to say now was occasioned by something the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) said in the course of his address yesterday. Mr. Bennett was beginning to see the need of reform in 1935. He declared that reform must come to the capitalist system, that something had to be done about the growing menace of unemployment. He was not allowed to carry into effect the reforms he had in mind-and I do not wish it to be said we knew or endorsed what he had in mind. I challenge anyone in this house today to show that since 1935 those fundamental weaknesses in the capitalist system, which Mr. Bennett appeared to see, have been removed, and that the necessary reforms have been carried out. They have not. No effort

at all has been made by the government that has been in office since that time to reform the fundamental weaknesses of the capitalist system and thereby make it possible for the Canadian people to have confidence in the future.
If that is the case-and I declare that it is -then these reforms must be undertaken at the earliest possible moment, and I am directing this question to my hon. friend the leader of the Conservative party. What fundamental reform of the capitalist system is there in the proposal he made here yesterday that we allow the thing to drift along, with works programs, the building of dams, power projects and irrigation systems? That is exactly the kind of thing that has been going on ever since Canada was Canada. Mr. Bennett appeared to know that works programs of that kind were not enough. I ask the leader of the Conservative party to stand up some time during the course of this debate and tell us where in this proposal is the fundamental reform that will take care of unemployment. It just is not there, as must be perfectly obvious to every thinking person.
Well, the question now before us is the Conservative amendment; and because it is some time since it was placed before the house I am going to deal with it clause by clause and tell the house what we think about it. The first clause reads:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that Your Excellency's advisers have:
(1) failed to take adequate measures to preserve and expand markets for Canada's surplus products of farm, forest, sea and mine, and to deal with the problems of increasing unemployment and reduced income to Canadian farmers and other producers.
We believe the statement in that first paragraph of the amendment represents the true situation today, and because that is so we are prepared to support that clause. I believe that in speeches already made by members of this group we have indicated how we feel about markets and surpluses. The truth of that matter is that we have lost our traditional British market; we have lost other traditional markets in the sterling area, and we have failed to protect the best interests of the Canadian people by well-timed, realistic action that would recapture those markets and preserve them for the future. The Liberal government have not played the game with the Canadian people. They have not played the game with the rest of the British commonwealth. That is why we supported the idea of a commonwealth conference on trade, suggested some time ago by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). We still feel that something worth while could be done through such a conference, to recapture and hold our traditional markets, and, while doing
The Address-Mr. Low so, strengthen our commonwealth ties. For these reasons we strongly supported that suggestion.
The other evening we were all pleased when the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew), on his return from a trip around the world, 'gave his realistic and refreshing speech on trade. Though he appears to have been forced to change what he originally said when he spoke in the house on March 13, as recorded at page 688 of Hansard, even in its changed form it makes an interesting and refreshing departure from the stubborn stand which the other ministers of the crown have taken and maintained during the past two or three years. I liked what the Minister of Fisheries said. I thought it indicated he had done some real and earnest thinking. What I am saying today is not to be interpreted in any way as criticism of the minister. I want to congratulate him upon his courage and his realism in standing up in this house and declaring to the Canadian people that there is a surplus problem, and an unemployment problem associated with it.
Anyone reading his speech cannot fail to get those two implications from it. In fact they are definite statements. He knew that surpluses and unemployment go together. He said so. In his prepared speech he saw to it that there was a hyphen placed between the two words; it is a surplus-unemployment problem. The Minister of Fisheries was realistic, honest enough, and felt his duties strongly enough, that he made that declaration to the Canadian people. I imagine the minister will have a hard time living down some of the things that did occur after he had made his speech. It is not going to be my purpose, however, to argue with him about the change he made.
I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, two or three things in the minister's speech which I believe he and his colleagues should follow up.
As recorded at page 688 of Hansard, the minister said:
Many of these difficulties may be overcome by extending the scope of barter arrangements for the particular commodities we have in surplus.
He indicated the reality of surpluses, and he indicated also a change from what we had heard a little while before the election of 1945. At that time the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), in a speech he delivered somewhere in southern Ontario, declared that the government was against barter deals. All through the election campaign the Liberals said that they were against barter deals. When the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) returned

The Address-Mr. Low from his recent journey to Europe he was reported in the Ottawa Citizen of March 2, page 19, column 1, paragraph 4, as follows:
Canada was encouraging private businessmen to arrange barter deals where such are more desirable. But the government was not directly involved in any such trade.
Even he, after a most stubborn stand over a period of almost two years, has finally come to the conclusion that Canada will have to resort to some barter. A realistic position will have to be taken to see to it that our trade constitutes largely an exchange of goods for goods, and that we are not restricted by this stupid convertibility provision. We want to see to it that goods are sold for convertible money as often as we can, but if our trade is going to be severely restricted by a convertibility clause in a trade agreement, then I say it is not realistic under present circumstances. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, as well as the Minister of Fisheries, has come to realize that we have to resort to some sort of barter in order to bring our trade up to the level we want. One other thing: I hope that the colleagues of the Minister of Fisheries will not be too stubborn about the situation in the future, but I hope he will be stubborn in maintaining his position.
Then, the Minister of Fisheries goes on to say this:
It seems possible, therefore, to work out in Canada a combination between the very large groups of manufacturers and wholesalers and the government to provide both the management and the finance-
I realize that that was changed, and I am admitting that here, so the minister will not think I am trying to twist what he said.
-to operate bilateral deals and to overcome the lack of facilities that faces any single corporation. Such a body could barter parcels of mixed Canadian merchandise for mixed imports from the nondollar countries, and such merchandise could of course include capital equipment as well as foodstuffs or raw materials.
The next paragraph reads as follows:
This instrument might be used experimentally as an additional means of meeting the surplus-unemployment problems. If the subject is not approached in some such way, there is a danger that the various boards handling surpluses will operate independently on a give-away basis, and that the various local unemployment problems will also be tackled by relief, public works or other means that will alleviate but not remove the basic difficulty.
Let me say that this suggestion put forward by the Minister of Fisheries is,- on a national scale, what the Social Credit group in this house has been advocating on an international scale for the past two years or more. It is an instrument by which surpluses of food and other materials might be exchanged between nations, to the mutual advantage of

those nations-an international commodity clearing house. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) says that such a thing is unnecessary now; that the government can handle the problem itself. It is not handling it. The problem is still here, and the surpluses are appearing, more and more in number and quantity. Unless we do adopt some such proposal as is represented by the international commodity clearing house, I am satisfied that the government of Canada is going to continue to find itself in the same embarrassing position, with respect to surpluses and unemployment, as it is in today, only more so. The sooner we get at it the better, because the international monetary fund and the international bank do not provide the mechanism for an exchange of goods and services between nations, except on a convertibility basis. This is impossible under the present circumstances, and will be until our sister nation, the United States, begins to make dollars available in sufficient quantity to make convertibility possible.
I just want to leave that part, Mr. Speaker, with this word to the Minister of Fisheries. I compliment him on his realism. It is a good sign, and it is certainly reassuring to me to know that at least one minister on the front benches sees through the film of money to the things that are beneath it.
Before I go on to the next subject, Mr. Speaker, there is one other thing that occurs to me about this matter of surpluses. I imagine that the Minister of Agriculture will never live down what he said the other night, "A little cheese, a little butter and some honey." It will be thrown up to him for quite some time. The ministers ought to be more straightforward than they have been about this matter of surpluses. They ought to let the Canadian people know just what the situation is. Surpluses began to appear in this country two years ago. Time after time, the government was warned about them, and about the danger of accumulating surpluses of goods and services. I know this group certainly warned the government on a number of occasions. I know the member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) warned the government on a number of occasions about what was happening in his constituency-the berry problem.
I was under the impression that there were surplus beans in this country. On March 1, the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. McCubbin), in answer to a question asked by the member for Middlesex East (Mr. White), told the house that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) arranged to give 38,000 bushels of beans to the refugees of the war in Palestine.

This cost the Canadian taxpayers $194,419.88. These had been bought under the Agricultural Prices Support Act. They were surplus, and there were given away. We would never have known about this magnanimous gesture on the part of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and his colleagues if a direct question had not been asked by the hon. member for Middlesex East. We suddenly found that there had been a surplus of beans in Canada, and the surplus had been cleared away by the expedient of the Secretary of State for External Affairs giving them away. I am not questioning for one moment the good purpose that was served. All I am suggesting is that surely hon. members ought to be given a chance of patting the minister on the back for his magnanimity on behalf of the Canadian people whose money bought up the surplus of beans. We should have been given an opportunity to pat the minister on the back and tell him what a good deed he had done with our money. That is all I am saying about this. But we were not informed. It is too bad that we missed such a chance in this house.

We now come to the third section of the Conservative amendment, and we wish to say that we can agree with it. It may not go quite far enough perhaps to suit some people, but we would support it. We would also support section 4. We did demonstrate last night what we thought about the extension. We can support the extension.
We now come to section 2. Section 2 has to do with the question of a contributory old age pension program. It refers to failure on the part of the government to inaugurate a contributory old age pension plan on a national scale. I should like to take the next few minutes to place before the house our views with respect to section 2.
We have not yet been convinced that it is possible under a free democracy to devise and apply a contributory scheme of old age pensions that would be socially just, or that could replace and render unnecessary a basic noncontributory scheme. If a contributory program of old age pensions is to be socially just, I think all hon. members can see that it must cover everybody in the nation. Any scheme of the kind that I have ever heard of is in most respects like the present unemployment insurance program that we have in Canada. Many classes of people are not covered by the insurance benefits, and indeed, sir, I cannot see how they can possibly be covered under any unemployment insurance scheme that is workable. Perhaps the best example of these classes is the farmer. How can contributions be collected from the farmers of this country for an old age pension scheme? Especially, sir, how can contributions be collected from that very large number of subsistence farmers, those who are living right on the borderline, and who may not have more than $50, $60 or $75 in cash in a year? In my judgment there will always be a substantial number of subsistence and marginal-line farmers who would not be able to make a contribution to any kind of an insurance scheme.
Just because they cannot, I ask this question: Are they to be denied the old age security that we are prepared to advance to other classes, especially to those who live and work in the cities? Will it be socially just to exclude the farmer who, along with his wife and family, today has to put in very long hours of labour, away beyond the limits of health in

The Address-Mr. Low jr my instances, ani to include on the other hand the organized workers who have succeeded in reducing hours of work to eight a day for a five-day week? Farmers have no five-day week and no eight-hour day.
Then, sir, there are those who are mentally or physically incapacitated, and therefore are permanently unemployable. How can these people become eligible to share in a contributory scheme of pension? And yet we all admit that something will have to be done to provide them with a means of living.
I was interested to hear the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) about a week ago say that he felt the kind of old age pension scheme we now have could not possibly be considered as anything else but contributory. I agree with him. The closest calculations that I have been able to make indicate that the average Canadian, who begins at twenty years of age his active earning life in this country under present conditions, pays to the federal government more than $54,000 in taxes by the time he has reached the age of seventy, and is therefore entitled to an old age pension. Some people call that merely good citizenship. We think it is more than that. It is also a very substantial premium on a decent old age pension.

Yes, as the hon. member suggests, if he has a chance to work. There is one aspect of this whole matter of pensions which I think all too often escapes notice. I refer to the fact that as more and more normal peacetime conditions return to our country and the world, and as more mechanization takes place throwing people out of work, it is possible to produce a very great volume of goods and services with less manhours of work than ever before.
As a result unemployment tends to spread. Consequently it becomes the practice to hire younger labourers and to turn the older ones away because they are too old to work. It is not exceptional in this country today to see men of fifty or fifty-five who are told, "We are not hiring men of your age." Much of this would not be so if our productive effort resulted in the distribution among consumers of enough purchasing power in the form of salaries, wages, dividends, profits and compensations to enable them to buy back what has been produced.
But that does not happen; and as a consequence surpluses of most things begin to accumulate that cannot be distributed because there is no money, or far too little, in the pockets of thousands of potential Canadian consumers. As this condition begins to develop it becomes possible to provide pensions to the aged without resorting to taxation. It can be done by having the treasury cause to be created new money to represent the actual value of the surpluses, which money is turned over to the health department to spend into circulation through pensions on a non-contributory basis. I contend such a procedure would save large quantities of goods and services that otherwise would be wasted, or that might remain unproduced.
The absolute necessity of adopting a procedure of this kind, Mr. Speaker, will become much more evident as general unemployment develops into a problem-and I say it will develop into a problem; there is no question about it.
I think one of the reasons why so many members of the house who favour better old age pensions do not cast their votes in favour of improvements when they are proposed by opposition groups on various occasions is that they fear the adverse effect

The Address-Mr. Low of the tax increases which would result. I do not think there is any question about that. For this they can hardly be blamed, because taxes bear too heavily now on the average Canadian.
What they can be blamed tor is that they have not sought out ways of improving our distribution system that has become so inefficient that it allows many hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of goods and services to go to waste each year, or to remain unproduced, which amounts to the same thing, if we can produce it. By a few fundamental changes in that wasteful distribution system it could be made possible for substantial improvements in the standard of old-age pensions without the necessity of increasing the tax load of the average Canadian. The Social Crediters try to see through the film of money to the realities that are beneath it. I know, Mr. Speaker, you are looking at me as if to indicate that my time has elapsed.

I certainly would not want to continue without the unanimous consent of the house, but I should like to take a moment to round out this argument because I think it is important to hon. members of the house. We look at Canada's almost limitless productive capacity. We see with regret apple trees pulled up by the roots, thousands of barrels of apples begging for someone to eat them; we see many hundreds of cases of healthgiving celery being dumped on the garbage heaps; all this because there are no buyers with cash to pay for these very important and worth-while products. We think of the ten per cent decline in poultry and egg production during the past few months. That decline could have been prevented if markets had been available.
Then we remember the 270,000 old age pensioners and the additional thousands of physically and mentally incapacitated Canadians who now are having to eke out a miserable existence on $40 or $50 per month, or even less in so many thousands of cases. I say to the members of this house: Could these aged citizens, could these mentally and physically incapacitated persons consume more of the products that are going to waste, either actually or because market incentives are not provided to have them produced? I think we must all agree that the answer to the question is obviously yes. I think we must all agree that the old age pensioners could and would consume these surpluses if they could get at them. It follows then that the problem is one

of bringing willing and needy consumers ana the actual or potential surplus production together. I emphasize that such a thing is physically possible.
Anyone who is at all well informed must know that whatever is physically possible and desirable can be made financially possible. We Social Crediters say that it must be made financially possible for our aged citizens to enjoy a decent standard of living because there is absolutely no reason in the world why the things to ensure that standard cannot be produced right here in our own country and made available to them. We look at the physical and natural realities. We conclude that it becomes our moral duty to see to it that our aged and incapacitated are not forced to continue to live in poverty while hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of good produce are allowed to waste.
While we keep these things in mind we Social Crediters think of the burdens carried by the taxpayers of this country. They must be protected as well. I venture the prediction that our aged Canadians and the thousands of crippled unemployables will never get social justice if it depends upon taxation to get it. I believe every thinking person realizes that that is so. While we are on this matter of taxation I should like to say just a word about the people who organize themselves to press for higher pensions. There is some responsibility upon them to find out what effect their pressure may have upon the taxpayers of Canada who are already overburdened by a heavy weight of tax exactions.

Mr. Speaker, at this late stage in the debate, I

shall only detain the house for five minutes. I am prompted to speak at all by a report which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press on March 7. It concerns income tax prosecutions against farmers on the prairies. I should like to draw this report to the attention of parliament, and particularly to the attention of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann). It reads as follows:
The national revenue department appears to be putting on another campaign against farmers who have failed to file income tax returns ... In the first two months of this year, 1,953 prosecutions have been launched, mainly in the prairie provinces and western Ontario.
The efficiency of the Department of National Revenue has been lauded in this House of Commons on many occasions. I believe most members are prepared to admit that the department is doing a capable and efficient job. So far as the current campaign is concerned, and others like it against the farmers, I think everyone would agree that the department was only doing its job, if the campaign were being conducted on a universal basis, that is, against all Canadian farmers and in all Canadian provinces. It is only fair that farmers, like everyone else, should pay their fair share of income taxes. However, according to this report, as well as other evidence which is available, the department is not conducting this campaign universally across the country. It seems to be concentrated on the prairies, and some provinces have been overlooked.
Investigations and prosecutions against farmers have been launched in the past several months, mainly in the prairie provinces. While there may have been some, I cannot find evidence of many prosecutions having been conducted in the other provinces, particularly in the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I have nothing against the farmers of Quebec. But I am using them as a basis of comparison for what is happening in Saskatchewan, my own province. I may be wrong, but this recent campaign appears to me to be discrimination against the prairie farmers. I ask the Minister of National Revenue to tell the people of Canada, as soon as he can, and particularly the farmers, why his department is so active against the farmers on the prairies, and so inactive against the farmers in Quebec and other provinces.

I want to discuss some problems of taxation, but particularly the problems of taxation dealing with urban and suburban municipalities. I hope to make one or two suggestions to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) which would, in my opinion, greatly ease the burden of taxation and the difficulties which we see only too plainly are facing our municipalities, particularly in Ontario, at the present time.
I wish to discuss particularly the municipalities in metropolitan areas. I am not referring to what are known as dormitory suburbs, but to those completely balanced municipalities which have grown on the perimeter of our major cities. I wish also to deal with the cities themselves.
The study I have made is of course of my own constituency of York West and the city of Toronto proper. I did this because it is the area I know best. The figures which I have obtained are, I believe, applicable to most of the municipalities in Canada which are growing in both population and industrial potential.
The dormitory suburb as such is now probably an uneconomical anachronism because today the cost of providing municipal services, schools, et cetera, to a house is so great that without adequate industrial assessment few municipalities can provide it and remain solvent. It is true there are several wealthy


suburban so-called villages without industry, where restrictions have been imposed on house construction, but these contain large houses and have a low density of population, there being in some cases only three to five houses to the acre; also the ratio of school-age children per house is below average simply because the residents are somewhat older and their families have grown up. Even so, these few expressly favoured municipalities are today faced with the most serious problems concerning the raising of revenue through taxation.
York West does not contain any such municipality and is in fact, despite its geographically suburban position, an industrial area, with a manufacturing output probably as large as any other constituency in the dominion.
The figures I wish to quote are taken from the taxation statistics of the Department of National Revenue. They are from the dominion bureau of statistics, and from the municipal taxes of the Department of Municipal Affairs in Ontario. While they are accurate in themselves, they deal with a slightly different period in time, and therefore the figures cannot be precise. But I submit they do not only indicate a trend, but are sufficiently accurate to prove the point which I wish to make at the present time. The interpretation of those figures, Mr. Speaker, I submit, shows the very serious situation which is facing municipalities at the present time.
Let me go over the district of which I have made a study. I am now referring to the riding of York West including the whole of the township of York, only about half of which is in my riding. These are the population figures for 1948: York township, 90,018; Etobicoke township, 30,769; Mimico, 10,164; New Toronto, 9,156; Swansea, 7,360; Weston, 7,219; Long Branch, 6,677; making a grand total for the riding of York West, with the addition I have mentioned, of 161,447. The population growth of this constituency, as estimated by many experts, is at an annual increase of 8 per cent. Therefore at the present time it is reasonable to assume that the district of York West has an estimated population of slightly over 187,000 people. By 1953, which is four years after the last election, and if there is no election in that year, that riding will have a population of over 225,000. If there is no election until 1954, the population will be approaching 240,000. I submit that, Mr. Speaker, to show the tremendous rate of growth of the suburban municipalities and the size of the district, which, as I say, comprises the riding of York West, and the peculiar problems which these municipalities are facing because of this growth.

I have here figures showing the total tax levy in York township, and the other municipalities. These figures are prepared by the Department of Municipal Affairs in Ontario, and appear in its annual report of municipal statistics for the year 1948. I believe that, with the consent of the house, these figures might be tabled. But, because of their interest, I shall give them in detail now. This table shows the total tax levy as compared with
the school tax, and the figures are Total Tax		as follows:

It is a burden which, because of the growth of population in that area, is increasing. It is also bound to increase further because of the extra services by way of schools and other physical services provided by municipalities when new population moves in.
Let us compare these levies with the figures showing income tax raised in the same district. These figures are from the statistical report for 1949 of the income tax branch. While the amounts for the district of West York are not broken down into municipalities, nor in fact are they broken down at all, they are based on returns for the Toronto metropolitan area of which the constituency of West York forms a part, despite the fact that it is not in the city of Toronto proper.
We have on the record a total municipal tax in West York of $6,012,753 and a total school tax of $2,029,816 for the year 1948. Thus it will be seen that the school tax is 33 per cent of the total tax levy, giving a per capita tax for municipal purposes of $37.30.
It is generally assumed that the average dwelling contains five people. Using that multiplier, as the standard for the family unit, we get a municipal tax per family unit, that is per house, of $185 for 1948. As I have said, taxes increased not only in 1949, but, I understand, are likely to increase again in 1950. So with a tax levy two years ago of $185 per house, the taxpayer in my constituency owning real property is bearing an increasingly heavy burden.
To realize just how heavy that burden is, let us compare these figures with the figures for income tax as applied to the Toronto metropolitan area. In that area there were
The Address-Mr. Adamson 359,119 taxable returns yielding a total tax of $115,400,000, or an average of $321 per taxpayer. These are the figures for 1947 when taxes were considerably higher than they are now, and exemptions lower. Out of a total population of 997,600 for the whole metropolitan area, this gives an average tax per income tax payer of $321.
In that year one out of every three citizens or residents in the Toronto metropolitan area -and in all cases I am taking the metropolitan area as the standard-paid income tax. I submit that with the increased exemptions the figure for this year is more likely to be one out of every four who would be liable for the payment of income tax. Also the tax collected would be considerably less than the $321 collected in 1947.
Let us see what this means. The municipal taxation on the householder, according to the figures I have given, amounted to $185. The average income tax was $321. Assuming that every householder is an income-tax payer, these figures show a municipal taxation of 54-5 per cent of total income taxation. In other words the average taxpayer in the Toronto metropolitan area is paying 54J per cent as much in municipal taxation as he is in income taxation. That, in my opinion, is a serious situation. It is a serious situation for a number of reasons. The first reason is that municipal taxation is a fixed charge on real property. If a citizen runs into hard times and his income decreases, his income tax also decreases, but his municipal tax continues and is a first charge against what may be his main security, namely, his house and his property.
That is the situation which I submit was largely responsible for the difficulties faced by the municipalities in the years following the first war. As property values fell, as they do in times of lowered national income, it became less and less desirable to own property. Many hundreds of people who were purchasing houses either on time payments or under a mortgage, found it was not economically sound to continue either type of payment because with the destruction of the value of real property they were better off to let the mortgage holder have the house and either purchase another house at a lower value or rent. That was the situation after the last war. We must prevent it from happening again.
With the tremendous increase in the number of new family units, particularly veterans' housing, in the constituency of York West, we are faced with a school problem of tremendous importance and seriousness. A veterans' housing project was erected in the township of Etobicoke consisting of some
808	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Adamson 350 houses. The qualification necessary to obtain a house was that you should be a veteran with overseas service and a minimum of two children. Actually each house rated 2-4 children, of whom two children were of school age. That meant that the school section was faced with the immediate problem of providing accommodation for from 600 to 700 children. With the optimum of 50 pupils per room that meant an additional ten or twelve rooms. At an average cost of $35,000 per room it meant that that school section was faced with an immediate capital outlay of from one-third to half a million dollars.
This was previously a farming district and it was absolutely impossible for that school section to make that capital outlay. It imposed a tremendous burden on the whole municipality. This is merely one example of the capital expenditures being faced by municipalities at the present ime. Admittedly the government of Ontario has done and is still doing a great deal to help in the erection of schools. In fact it would be impossible for many municipalities to go ahead with their school building programs if it were not for the aid being given by the provincial government.
The figures I have given to the house indicate the tremendously heavy burden of taxation that is being borne, a burden which is likely to grow. I suggest that the ratio of municipal taxation to the federal income tax is now nearly 60 per cent in many sections. That is assuming that the householder and the income-tax payer is one and the same person, and that is true in virtually all cases.
A principle was enunciated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in his last budget against double taxation. He wisely-and I would like to see this extended-made a deduction of ten per cent on income from dividends paid by Canadian corporations. That was a step in the right direction and I hope in the budget to be brought down it will be extended. But here is an even more vicious example of double taxation. The home owner has a liability to pay municipal taxes which is just as much a liability as a mortgage would be. Unless he pays, he loses his property. Yet he gets no credit in his income tax return for that payment. For income tax purposes he is not allowed to deduct those essential taxes he pays to the municipalities. Nor is he allowed under the regulations as I understand them to deduct mortgage payments on his own home. My just request therefore is that municipal taxation be considered as a deductible expense for income tax purposes.


There is one other and slightly increased danger to the man or family buying their own home today under a long-term program extending over twenty, twenty-five, thirty, and in some cases forty years. The payments being made are a direct charge against the family. If they are not made, the security of the home owner is destroyed because he loses his property.
I have one further suggestion to make as to education. Today the cost of education to municipalities and taxpayers of municipalities is a matter of growing concern. As I have shown, it is fully one-third of the total tax levy at the present time. Here is a direct charge for the education of our children which must be met. If I as a taxpayer give a scholarship to educate somebody else's child I am allowed to deduct that from my income for taxation purposes. Nevertheless, because it is my moral responsibility to educate my own child, I am not allowed to make a deduction from my own income for that purpose. I suggest that the matter should not be placed on a moral basis. It should be placed on an actuarial or economic basis. It is much more important for me to see that the children who are my responsibility receive as good an education as they are capable of absorbing. Because it is my duty to do so, and because I will endeavour to do so, is beside the point. I feel that the government should base its taxation so that the money spent by an individual taxpayer for the education of his children by way of school taxes or school or university fees should be allowed as a deduction from his income for taxation purposes.
I have tried to show the house that our system of municipal taxation is a growing burden on the very people who form the backbone of the country, the great middle class, the people who own their own homes, who are doing everything to maintain the economic stability of the country, the people who should be encouraged in every conceivable way to do the very thing they are doing, namely, build a house, live in it, have a family and form a stable and secure backbone of the economy of Canada. Therefore I suggest to the Minister of Finance that in the preparation of the budget one of the reforms that should be included is that taxation levied by way of municipal taxes on the homes and properties of taxpayers should be allowed as a deduction from income for taxation purposes. Municipal taxation is a liability just as much as the interest payments on borrowed money.
As I have indicated, in my riding the total of such taxes in 1948 amounted to some $6 million. The loss of revenue would therefore not be a great one, and it would be an immedi-

ate help not only to the municipality but also to the home owner.
Today municipalities in the constituency of West York are submitting resolution after resolution to me asking that the federal government assume 50 per cent of the cost of direct relief. With these resolutions I am in complete accord, but I suggest that the two recommendations I have made would be of immediate help to municipalities and home owners. In accepting these suggestions we would not be doing anything but admitting and continuing the principle that dual taxation is an evil. We would be providing that branch of government which is closest to the people, municipal government, with a degree of security, and by the adoption of the two suggestions I have made we would provide home owners, heads of families, with a sense of growing security and a realization that to own a home, to have a family, is something which is the foundation of our economic system and is the highest type of action any citizen can take. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that these two recommendations should be given earnest attention by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) when considering any new measures of taxation to be included in the budget he will be bringing down shortly.

First, may I explain my reason for participating in this debate. During the last session, I spoke briefly during our discussion of amendments to the National Housing Act and confined my remarks at that time to the housing situation. I therefore wish to take advantage of this debate to mention briefly other matters of concern to our people.
May I join the speakers preceding me and congratulate the mover and seconder, Mr. Larson and Mr. Dumas, for the very capable manner in which they discharged their duties, and further may I add a word of congratulation, late perhaps but none the less sincere, to our new Minister of Citizenship and Immigration who, I am sure, will give his new department the splendid leadership it deserves.
During the long history of parliament it has been the privilege of hon. members taking part in this debate to eulogize their own constituencies. It is not my intention to follow that practice; in fact I do not think I will mention my riding at all. Mind you, I could use the entire forty minutes allotted to me in telling you of this grand district of Nipissing which I have the pleasure to represent, strategically located as it is at the gateway to the unlimited wealth of our great north land. I could tell you of the great resources of this district; I could give you some of the highlights of the history of some of the centres of population in my riding. I could tell 55946-52
The Address-Mr. Garland you stories of the picturesque and beautiful town of Mattawa, nestled in the valley at the junction of the Mattawa and Ottawa rivers. Or I could tell you the history of Sturgeon Falls and how it became a boom town with the building of the Abitibi mill there; of its history during the long, dark years of depression, and its resurgence as one of the best towns in northern Ontario. I could tell you of North Bay, so properly called the gateway to the north and the capital of northern Ontario. I could tell you that North Bay is a great transportation city, because all the commerce of the north must pass our way.
I could tell you of the railways fanning out in all directions, carrying manufactured goods from the south to house, clothe and feed the people of northern Ontario and northwestern Quebec, and bringing from our great north country the materials wrought from our rich and bountiful land, products of the forests and the mine, including gold, silver, cobalt and nickel. Yes; 95 per cent of the world's supply of nickel is produced only some eighty miles west of our city. Busses, too, fan out in all directions from our city, over a splendid system of highways, carrying people to and from the industrial centres to the south and to the mining and lumber districts of the north. We have, also, one of the finest airports in the country.
Then, if I chose, I could tell you of the hundreds of lakes and streams so bountifully stocked with every fish imaginable that have attracted and are continuing to attract thousands of tourists to our district. I could tell you of the miles of beautiful sand beaches on lake Nipissing, that same sandy shore where the famous explorer Champlain paused with his friend, Brule, in the long twilight of a summer evening on that 25th day of July, 1615, and admired the beauty of this great inland lake. I could tell you, if I were not so hesitant to boast of our district, that here in lake Nipissing is the greatest pickerel fishing bank on the North American continent; I could also invite you to come to Nipissing and paddle your canoe over the beautiful waters of Trout lake and travel, if you will, the exact course taken by Champlain on that day so long ago on what is now known to thousands as the famous Champlain trail. Then I could tell you of the beautiful Temagami area in the north end of my riding, rapidly developing into one of Canada's most popular summer playgrounds. I could tell you of the wonderful possibilities of the beautiful French river area, as yet practically virgin territory.
Yes, if I were not so hesitant to extol the virtues of my riding, I could tell you that this great paradise attracts thousands of tourists annually, who swell our population and spend

The Address-Mr. Garland approximately $5 million each year in our district. Then, if I chose, I could tell you of our people; I could tell you that Nipissing is the home of the world-famous Dionne quintuplets, those five charming young ladies who only a few years ago rocketed our little village of Corbeil into international headlines; I could tell you of our people, English-speaking, French-speaking, people of Italian origin, and so on, who, regardless of their race or background, are real Canadians with a tremendous amount of faith in the future of our great country.
All this I could tell you and more if, as I said before, I were not so hesitant to boost my riding. I would extend a welcome to industry planning new developments to seriously consider the district of Nipissing before making any final decision as to the location of new plants, because Nipissing is the geographical centre of Ontario, linking northern and southern Ontario. To our west lie the sprawling grain empire of the prairies and the rapidly-developing oil fields of western Canada; and to our east the great port cities of the Atlantic. In these days when so much emphasis is being placed upon decentralization, I would urge that consideration be given to our district. Here employer and employee can work and live together, removed from the countless pitfalls of congested-area living, yet only a few hours away from the great markets provided by Canada's large cities.
And now, sir, I turn to other matters. I was indeed pleased to see our government, during the last session, acknowledge their responsibility regarding assistance to municipalities where there is an excess of federal buildings. While the government is to be commended, I do not believe that we have gone far enough, because regardless of the concentration of these federal buildings the responsibility is there, and I hope that the legislation proposed last year and again referred to in the speech from the throne this session is only the thin edge of the wedge, and that our government will give further consideration to this assistance to our hard-pressed municipalities.
Now, sir, a word about social security measures in general and old age security in particular. I am indeed pleased, as I feel sure all hon. members are, to see a committee being set up to study thoroughly all phases of an adequate old age security measure. We have heard considerable talk in this country about the abolition of the means test, and I regret to see some of our people using this issue to stir up worry and discontent, yes, even hardship, among our older people, knowing full well that they do not have the

authority or the responsibility of doing anything about it. Unfortunately there are two groups of people in this country-one who would recommend giving everything to the people with no regard to the cost, and the other who shudder when the words "social security" are mentioned. They hide behind the cloak of free enterprise and claim that any step forward in the field of social security is a sign of weakness and can only result in the softening and breaking down of the initiative of our people. Thank goodness there is still a third group, to which I subscribe, who do not believe that everyone should be dependent upon the state, nor on the other hand that business exists only for the sake of business and profits. We believe that industry can and should show a profit and yet, at the same time, can and should share some of these profits with labour. These same beliefs, it would seem, carry through when thinking in terms of old age security. One group would recommend pensions for everyone without restrictions; another group believe that the government has gone too far with its present legislation, and in our own group we believe that the whole matter should be gone into very thoroughly and similar types of legislation in other countries studied, and in gathering these facts making sure that any new plans being embarked upon can be carried out successfully and within the means of Canada's national purse. Let us all join together in working out a plan whereby Canada's senior citizens may be freed forever from anxiety and fear; that will enable them to relax and enjoy, in the twilight years of their life, the peace and security they so richly deserve.
At this time, I should like to refer briefly to a matter that has not been covered, to my knowledge, by other hon. members, and that is Canada's tourist industry. During 1949, Canada's tourist industry established new records, when over-all revenues from travellers from other countries reached $288 million according to the bureau of statistics. Today, the tourist business provides more United States dollars to Canadian people than any other export industry, with the sole exception of newsprint. It is, therefore, no mean factor in our national economy. This industry depletes no raw materials in this country, because our forests and streams, our fish and game, can be preserved by intelligent conservation methods for generations to come. The tourist business, in the main, consists of accommodation and personal services for several million travellers each year; travellers who return to their own countries as the most effective ambassadors of good will it is possible to obtain.
Both 1948 and 1949 have been record tourist years. There are signs, however, that

the days of the easy tourist dollars are disappearing. Competition in the travel business is friendly, but is none the less intense. In the year 1948, for instance, tourist promotion agencies in the state of California spent over $900,000 on advertising and publicity, more than the entire advertising appropriation of the Canadian government travel bureau. In that same year, other states of the union spent over $5 million on travel promotion on their own behalf. In addition to this United States competition, Canada must face competition provided by some 46 foreign governments which maintain travel promotion offices in the United States.
The advertising budget allotted to the Canadian government travel bureau to further this important industry, our second ranking source of United States dollars, was $820,000 for the 1948-49 fiscal year. It is $895,000 for the 1949-50 fiscal year, or less than one-third of one per cent of the annual revenues. All Canadian travel promotion organizations, including the travel bureau, the provincial tourist bureaux, railways, steamship lines, and other transportation interests last year spent $2,500,000 on advertising in the United States, or less than one per cent of the 288 million United States dollars the tourist industry brought into this country. Considering the size of the job, and the amount of money available, the Canadian government travel bureau's advertising campaign has had results which in many respects have been phenomenal. In 1949 the bureau handled 321,751 individual inquiries. The tourist industry of this country broke all its previous records in both 1948 and 1949, and it now looms large in the Canadian economy.
This travel movement across the United States border is far from being one way, however. The success of our competitors' own advertising is demonstrated by the alltime high of travel spending by Canadians in other countries in 1949. They spent $164 million on pleasure travel in the United States during the year, according to the bureau of statistics, and $27 million in other countries. This total of $191 million was a new record. Travel business is not restricted in importance to those directly engaged in serving the tourist. It is a business which puts new money into the pockets of every Canadian, whether he be a farmer, a railroader, in fact, everyone, because everyone depends upon the general prosperity of our country for their livelihood. It puts money into the treasury of our federal government, and every provincial government in this country. It seems fair to suggest that this important industry's welfare is the concern of every Canadian.
The Address-Mr. Garland
We have a wonderful country to offer on the travel markets of the world. It has a land area of three and a half million square miles, with more than half of the world's fresh water; a wealth of scenic beauty; rich reserves of fish and game, and an incredibly varied climate. Perhaps because of this, the travel business is one which does a very respectable job of furthering its own growth; however, that does not mean it merits the neglect which it sometimes encounters in the minds of those who take it for granted. In such a competitive business, this is an unwise, even a dangerous attitude. A business that brings more than a quarter billion of new money into this country in a single year calls for the same kind of realistic attention we give our other export activities.
We must remember also that our problem with respect to the United States, which is the greatest travel market in the world, is a peculiar one. The average Canadian knows a great deal about events in the United States; he cannot help it when he reads his newspapers, his magazines or listens to his radio. Unfortunately, he does not always realize how little the average citizen of the United States knows of affairs in Canada; yes, indeed, how little his neighbours know of the simple geography of this country. Therefore, the travel business does both a public relations job and an information job for Canada.
Our game and fish, our forests, all help tell the Canadian story in the simplest and most fundamental manner. The courtesy of our people to the yearly influx of vacationseeking visitors is becoming a byword across the border. It has done much to sell Cana-dianism in the United States, but it is a story that needs telling in many different forms, and none of them deserve neglect or indifference. We shall never fully realize the value of the tourist industry to this country until the day when it might be lost. That day will never come if due attention is paid to this basic enterprise. So I would urge the government to pay special attention to the development of this very important industry. True, the government is assisting in various ways. One could not cite a better example than the completion of the trans-Canada highway. Surely nothing is more important to our visitors than good roads. But, I repeat, the Canadian story needs telling in many ways. This government can do this by extending the budget of our Canadian travel bureau; and in so doing broaden its facilities. It is my prediction and my sincere hope that, in the not too distant future, the Canadian travel hureau will have an annual budget of $5

The Address-Mr. Knowles million, and our tourist industry will be pulling a billion United States dollars into Canada every year.
