speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I wish to say again what I have said before, that I give credit to the federal government for the soundness of the proposal they made in 1945. I have said it a good many times, and I hope my approval of it is not turning the government away from it. The people of Canada still remember it, and agree with it. Indeed there is an essential soundness in the original proposal. It needs to be amended in really only one important particular-as to the amount. That $30 figure of 1945, when taking into con-
The Address-Mr. Knowles sideration the rise in the cost of living index from 1945 to 1950, should now be something over $40.
So all the government has to do to have a sound proposal to put before the country today is to take the proposals of 1945, amend the $30 figure to $40 and give to the people of Canada an old age pension of at least $40 a month payable to all at age seventy, without a means test. Then the other proposal is still there for pensions for those from sixty-five to sixty-nine as well.
For a few years we heard a good deal about the alleged refusal of some of the provinces to enter into a tax agreement. We were told many times that that was the reason those proposals could not be put into effect. We do not hear so much about that today. I wonder if it is because of the pleasant atmosphere of the conference which took place in this chamber in January of this year. Prior to that the government could always talk about the fact that two provinces had refused to agree, and that always seemed to be a sufficient alibi-at least to the government. Today, however, it appears that the provinces are a little more friendly to the idea of finding ways and means of adjusting our dominion-provincial difficulties. We do not hear so much about that phase of the matter now. We hear, rather, the sort of remark that we heard from the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) and again this afternoon from the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Garland) that you have to consider the cost involved, and that you have to consider whether or not the government ever offered old age pensions without a means test, unless there was attached to it a contribution, which I have dealt with on a previous occasion.
It was very clear in the 1945 proposals that any financing that would have to be done was to be done by a modification of the income tax. There was to be no constitutional change -and I am sure when the government said in 1945 that there was to be no constitutional change it had in mind the fact that back in 1925 the Department of Justice had given the federal government a ruling, and that that ruling was that you could not impose a special tax for social security purposes without having an amendment to the constitution.
So the government in 1945 no doubt had that ruling in mind when it said, "we have worked out a scheme which can be implemented without any constitutional change." They also said in 1945, and repeated it in 1946 and 1947 and 1948, that those proposals were worked out on the basis of considerable study, and that it was a plan that would hold together and work.
814	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Knowles
That proposal, in effect, is what is before us in the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), because in his subamendment he asks us to change the wording of the main amendment before us so that we will be voting for a national system of old age pensions, without a means test.
The amendment of the hon. member also draws particular attention to the use of the word "contributory". I think it is valuable that there has been a great deal of discussion in the house and in the press and throughout the country about that word. I think a great deal more discussion is necessary, and a great deal more thinking before some hon. members get it all sorted out. In my view it is a word that is being used sloppily, and for various motives.
I wish to support the views expressed this afternoon by the hon. member for Peace River when he said that the only way in which we can pay for social security at any time is out of current production. He made that very clear this afternoon-and it is exactly what the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) has said a number of times. By the way, I commend the remarks of the hon. member for Peace River to his colleague the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell), because he did not seem to like what was said the other evening by the hon. member for Vancouver East. However, that is only by the way.
That point must be driven home, and we must think about it. It is fundamental to the whole concept of social security; because when today old age pensioners are living on their old age pensions, or when people are living on pensions from private industry, or from civil service pensions, or whatever it may be, they are not living on dollars and cents; they are not living on pieces of paper; they are living on a portion of the production of today's economy. What we are doing is to permit a portion of current production to be used for a socially desirable objective-to provide some sort of retirement for some of our older people.
The tragedy is that we have not reached the point where we can decide as a nation that we are going to set apart a sufficient portion of the production we are now producing to provide adequate retirement for all our old people. Similarly in the year 1990 or 2000 A.D., as the hon. member for Peace River said this afternoon, people who are now 20 or 30 will be retiring. They will not live on credits in some insurance office, or at the annuities branch, or in some new office where records are kept. They will not live on dollars and
fMr. Knowles.]

cents, on cheques, or paper; they will live on goods and services out of the production that is current in the year 1990 or in the year 2000.
The reason it is important for us to realize all this is so that we will not use this word "contributory" in a sloppy fashion. Too many members in the house seem to think there is some magic in that word. They seem to have in mind that if individuals, on a contract basis, put aside so many dollars a month or so many dollars a year, across the years, in some magic way they will be able to retire without a means test when their working years are done.
Well, as the hon. member for Peace River pointed out, that depends upon the economy of that day, the value of the dollar in that day and, in the final analysis, upon what society in that day is producing. That means this, that the only use of the word contributory that is realistic is as it is used in current terms. We are all contributing today to old age security, such as it is, which some of our old people enjoy. We contribute to it out of the wealth being produced today. And when some of us are old and retired, if we are on an old age pension at that time, we will be enjoying a portion of what is produced at that time and contributed to our retirement, in the goods and services we will consume, by the people who are working in that day.
The quid pro quo of this is that people who are working today should in any decent and sensible society contribute toward the security of people who need it today and, in turn, we will get the same consideration from the people who are working when our day comes to retire, and so on. I plead with hon. members to think of this whole business of social security in those terms rather than in the private life insurance company terms which envisage people simply paying contributions into a fund and somehow magically being able to retire at a later year.
As a matter of fact I hold in my hand the current tables of the annuities branch which are contained in sessional paper 64-A tabled on Wednesday, March 8, of this year. It occurred to me that it might be interesting to look into this to see what it would cost on an annuity basis for a person 25 years of age to try to provide for retirement 40 years from now on a direct contributory basis. Surely that is a long enough period in the twentieth century to ask people to work.
If a young man 25 years of age wishes to try to provide an annuity of $100 per month at 65, which I hope would not be unreasonable for a man and wife 40 years from now, the rate for males would be $15.24 per month, which would have to be paid every month

for 40 years. If a woman aged 25 years was seeking to provide $100 per month at age 65 she would have to pay $17.64 per month for 40 years. If you think in terms of a man and wife both aged 25 years who are seeking to buy an annuity of $50 each so that they would have $100 as long as they were both living and $50 when there was only one survivor, the average of the figures I have given would amount to $16.44 per month for the 40 years.
Even if you put it on a split basis and divide the cost among employer, employee and the government on a 40-40-20 basis- I use that figure not to propose it but simply because it is the unemployment insurance basis-you would be asking people to contribute $6 or $7 per month for 40 years, and employers to do the same. That amount would be the required contribution to a contributory scheme on a direct individual basis. In terms of the wage rates of our people, in terms of the income of farmers across the years, it would be impossible to impose such a payment on all our people. Those who are saying that we cannot afford to remove the means test without putting it on a contributory basis might as well realize that they are saying to the people of this country that we cannot get rid of the means test. If you are putting it on a direct contributory basis, the cost to the individual is clearly prohibitive.
Someone may ask, and it is a fair question: If you cannot do it that way, how are you going to do it? The fact is that if you are going to have a proper retirement allowance for old people, bearing in mind that the people cannot pay for it themselves out of the wages they are now getting, what you absolutely have to have is a certain amount of redistribution of wealth in favour of social security. The justification for a redistribution of wealth in favour of social security is that people who are earning wages of $30 or $40 a week cannot afford to buy their own old age security and yet they are producing wealth far in excess of what they are getting. I assert that those who are trying to push forward an individual direct contributory idea are simply trying to stem the tide of the redistribution of wealth in social terms such as I am suggesting to the house right now.
I urge strongly that members face up to these facts and realize that the only possible way to get proper social security is to build it into the income tax structure whereby people will pay for the total cost of government, including social security, on the basis of ability to pay and then, as a matter of
The Address-Mr. Knowles right, draw their pensions when retirement is reached.
That is our position. It is because of that philosophy, it is because of that analysis, which I submit is fundamentally sound, that I take up the time of the house at this stage of the debate to urge the government to consider the fact that they should be bringing in a proposal to amend the Old Age Pensions Act in such a way as to eliminate the means test and put it on a universal basis. I ask the government to go back and read their own material submitted to the dominion-provincial conference. I ask them to read their own assertions that amendments to the constitution were not necessary, that a plan had been worked out on the basis of study, a plan that would work, and that it would be brought into effect with the least possible delay.
This afternoon the hon. member for Nip-issing (Mr. Garland) made a most interesting speech and I think we all enjoyed the way in which he was so hesitant about telling us of the beauties of his constituency. Apart from that he went on to say that those who were advocating the removal of the means test were bringing hardship and misery to our older people. May I tell him that the hardship and misery that our older people are suffering is more real than that; it is the reality of the means test that is really hurting them. They are suffering, too, from the kind of thing that is being said in newspapers and in this house which leads them to believe that they are not going to be relieved of the means test unless the plan is put on a contributory basis. I do not know whether many people have seen annuity tables such as those I hold in my hand, but even if they have never seen such figures they realize that with the incomes they get they simply cannot afford to make the contributions necessary to provide for their old age security.
In the light of what I have said, it is obvious that we shall support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River. I think all hon. members in the house should support it, and I think that Liberals in particular should support it because it gives them a chance to vote for the old age pension proposal of 1945 which they reiterated with such fanfare in their national convention of 1948.
I said earlier that I rose for at least one other reason, and I turn now to deal with it. I hold in my hand a couple of press reports, both written by the same writer but appearing in different papers. They both refer to a speech I made in this house during this same debate, back on March 6. One report appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of Thursday, March 9, 1950, under the byline of Chester Bloom, and the other appeared in the
816	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Knowles Free Press Weekly Prairie Farmer of March 15, 1950, also written by Chester Bloom. The article in the Winnipeg Free Press reads: Pension Issue Bares Rift in C.C.F. Party By Chester Bloom
Ottawa, March 9 (Special)-Mr. M. J. Coldwell, C.C.F leader, Wednesday attempted to smooth over indications of splintering in the C.C.F. group in the House of Commons.
The general C.C.F. policy has been to go along with the Liberal government against the Progressive Conservatives on questions involving expansion of social security.	_
Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) Monday seemed' to strive to create a direct breach with the St. Laurent cabinet. Again and again, he berated the Prime Minister for allegedly breaking the "promise" of August, 1945, of old age pensions for those 70 years and over without means test. He included other ministers in the attack.
The article goes on to suggest that there is a rift or division between my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), and me over this issue. The irony of this story is that when you compare the quotations from my speech and from what my leader said there is no difference whatsoever. Mr. Bloom goes on to state:
Mr. Coldwell said Wednesday his party's platform backed the contributory plan but only on an overall basis-that is, including health, sickness benefits, hospitalization, unemployment insurance and old age pensions without a means test.
The party did not want old age pensions put on a contributory basis separately from the other social security planks.
That is exactly the position that I took; indeed it is exactly the position that Chester Bloom says I took. He said that I gave the impression we are pulling away from supporting the Liberal party because while we support a contributory over-all social security plan we are not prepared to accept a contributory one-point social security plan. That is exactly my position, the position of my leader, the position of this group and of this party. I suggest that sort of journalism is not very responsible, especially when the story fails to bear out the heading and the opening paragraph.
In the same article Mr. Bloom says:
Mr. Knowles carefully avoided mentioning that this so-called "promise" actually was a proposal conditional on all provinces accepting the complex dominion-provincial agreements of 1945.
May I ask Mr. Bloom to look at pages 472, 473 and 474 of Hansard for March 6, and he will find that on at least three occasions I referred to the fact that the original proposals had been based on the tax agreements, but I pointed out-and this was my complaint -that the government was no longer using the refusal of certain provinces to agree to these taxation arrangements as its excuse for not going ahead, but rather it was now saying


that it had never proposed old age pensions without a means test except on a contributory basis.
Not content with that irresponsible and completely erroneous story about a rift in this party over the question of social security, which it is really ludicrous to even suggest, Mr. Bloom rewrote his article in a longer story which appeared in the Free Press Weekly Prairie Farmer of March 15, 1950, and he really went overboard this time. The heading is:
They say at Ottawa.
The subheading is:
Mr. Knowles re-words the communist doctrine.
Things have got to a pretty bad state in this country when you have to start throwing the word "communist" at a person because he advocates the removal of the means test from old age pensions. That is just how bad it is. I am amazed at even the Free Press doing that. The last time they used the word "communist" in connection with my" name they apologized within two days. Mr. Bloom not only repeats part of what he said in the article in the daily Free Press but also goes on to say:
Actually, the most important utterance of Mr. Knowles can be found on page 475 Hansard, March 6 last. How close C.C.F. speakers approach communist doctrine in the heat of debate was illustrated by that remark. Mr. Knowles said he believed (his own opinion) -
It is substantiated by the green books I have on my desk.
-that the federal government in the dominion-provincial agreement proposals of 1945 had in mind adjustments or increases in the income tax to pay the total cost of old age pensions without a means test out of the federal treasury. Then he added-
This next paragraph is in black face type, in quotation marks, and is directly from me.
"That would be a proper scheme because it would envision people paying according to their ability to pay and drawing the old age pensions at the proper age as a matter of right."
That is the end of Mr. Bloom's quotation from me, and the next paragraph reads:
That phrase, obviously, is merely a rewording of the fundamental Marxian communist doctrine: "From him according to his ability and to him according to his need." Realistically, it means taking the property and possessions of people who have them andi giving them to people who do not have them.
I should like Chester Bloom and others to note the paragraph which he quoted from what I said, and by which I stand as a statement of something fundamentally sound. Then I should like him to compare it with this statement which I am now going to read. It is as follows:
What we mean by a contributory old age pension scheme is a scheme whereby all Canadians will contribute each year to a fund for old age pensions

and where old age pensions will be paid out as a matter of right to those who will have attained the pensionable age.
That is exactly the same doctrine, that all of us should pay into a fund and that we should then draw our pensions as a matter of right at the pensionable age. This speaker went on to spell it out even more clearly. He said:
Some of us won't have long to go-
This man is in his late sixties.
-and won't have many payments to make before we get ours, but it is a system that will go on continuously and will mean no unfairness to those who will start at the age of twenty or twenty-one and who will continue to pay into the fund until they reach pensionable age. It will be a pension of an equal amount for everyone at pensionable age to which everyone of taxable age will make a direct contribution.
There it is, another way of stating exactly what I said, that what is meant by a proper old age pension scheme is one into which we all pay, all of us who are taxable, all of us who can afford it whether we are sixty-eight or twenty-one, and in return for having played our part in contributing to the providing cf social security in the days when we were working, when we reach pensionable age we draw a pension as of right at a flat amount, the same amount for everybody, without a means test.
I ask Chester Bloom this question. If he insists on saying to the people of western Canada that my statement was a rewording of communist doctrine will he not say the same for the statement I have just quoted, which is that of the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) speaking in Vancouver on April 14, 1949? The statement he made was not something the Liberal party wanted to forget because they gave it permanent form in the fall issue of their quarterly publication, The Canadian Liberal. The fact is that both statements are fundamentally sound.
I submit again that this sort of journalism is the kind that brings freedom into danger, and that even the Free Press should not indulge in that sort of thing. When these articles first appeared I thought of rising in the house on a question of privilege, but I felt that perhaps it deserved even more than that. To return to what I said earlier, I want to add that what bothers me about articles of this kind is not only the irresponsible journalism involved therein, and the misstatements to which I have drawn attention, but also that what is going on here is an attempt in many papers-I saw it in the Globe and Mail a few days ago-to tell the people of Canada that they cannot have the removal of the means test until our whole pension plan is put on a direct contributory
The Address-Mr. Knowles contract basis. If we have to wait for that we will never get it, at least not for all our people. If we have to wait' for that you have to think in terms of the figures I gave from the annuity tables. If you are thinking of that you are asking for the kind of system they have in the United States where, despite some of its good features, it is providing, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) said the other day, only ten per cent of their retired people with a pension as of right, leaving many thousands still on a means test basis.
In other words, it all adds up to the clear position that if there is to be one next step, as is the case in practical politics, that next step should be the removal of the means test from the present old age pension. Let us have along with it, if we possibly can, the lowering of the age, but certainly let us have a revision of that $30 figure of 1945 into a figure of at least $40 for 1950. I call upon the government of the day to implement the sound proposal they made at that time.

speechtext: I know that hon. members are calling "time", and I am going to sit down shortly. Nevertheless I suggest to hon. members that they think very clearly before they vote on the amendment to the amendment of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) because what they are being asked to vote on is their own government's proposal of 1945, reiterated in their convention of 1948, promised to the people of their constituencies in 1949, and promised by many of them in the language the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Campney) used when he said that he would fight for it here in this house. I suggest the least they can do is vote for it when they get the chance to do so.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this particular portion of the debate has been headed, as hon. members know, by the amendment of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) which in the first place strikes out the word "contributory" from the Conservative amendment, indicating that Social Crediters are opposed to the contributory idea in respect of old age pensions and social security, and especially old age pensions which are under discussion at the present time. The last portion of our amendment reads:
The government has . . . failed to adopt measures adequate to establish in our country a balanced economy wherein Canadian consumers are constantly supplied with effective purchasing power sufficient to enable them to buy Canada's total production, if they so desire.
I am inclined to think this particular portion of the amendment sets us at variance

The Address-Mr. Blackmore would say there were surplus goods, $15 billion worth of them, which would serve as a backing for the creation of debt-free money. I think that makes quite clear what is meant by Social Crediters, when they speak of the creation of money out of production. They do not mean stealing it out of the pockets of the people who are toiling to produce, because that only decreases the purchasing power in the country, and makes the whole economy worse off.
The member for Peace River (Mr. Low) mentioned this afternoon money for old age pensions, and I shall try to interpret what he said. The member is sitting right here, so he can testify as to whether or not this is what he meant. When he spoke of getting money by deduction out of production, he meant that the money saved up for old age pensions say over 20 years, starting say in 1950, will be spent in say 1970, thereby using part of the production of 1970. May I ask the member for Peace River, in your presence, Mr. Speaker, if that is so.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is true.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is another meaning entirely than the one which the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) took from the hon. member's remark.
Now I desire tonight, in the time at my disposal, to discuss the whole question of sound money. We have to face this thing first or last, Mr. Speaker, and we had better face it first. It should be faced right now. If there is not any truth in the social credit contention, then we invite the 262 members of this house to prove it. The case is clear, and hon. members are welcome to say anything they desire. If we cannot answer every one of their questions, then it will be time for them to wonder whether our ideas about sound money are correct. In the meantime, we are going to talk about sound money.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Try to prove that your money is sound first, and then we shall listen to you attentively.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Good, I think we shall prove it to you. In fact, I think I have proved it already by the illustration of the $45 billion and the $60 billion in the United States, and the illustration about the $450 million in greenbacks in Lincoln's time. I believe all reasonable men will admit that is proof.
May I begin by quoting from the words of our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), as they appear at page 58 of Hansard:
And that is not just a problem of convertibility.
He is talking about taking sterling in return for our goods.
The dollars or pounds are merely symbols;

After quoting from the Prime Minister, may I draw this conclusion? If money is only a symbol of goods, and we now have more goods in Canada than we have symbols to distribute, why can we not create the symbols without borrowing them from the bank or anybody else? The bank creates them, and then we borrow them and put ourselves in debt by paying interest to the bank. Because we do not feel free to borrow enough, we cannot pay our old age pensioners what they ought to have.
Some discussion is going on in the country now about money. We notice this year that the Financial Post has stepped into the picture, trying to discredit what the Social Crediters are going to say, before they had a chance to speak. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) dealt with that in his first speech.
Now we have the Toronto Star Weekly, an admirable paper in many respects, probably quite honest-I am assuming it is quite honest-in its February 25 issue carrying an article by Robert Nielsen from Ottawa, so it is supposed to be authentic. This article is called "It's only money." May I quote several passages from Mr. Nielsen's article? Near the beginning he says, in speaking of the history of Canadian money:
In. the intervening four centuries, there have been more kinds of funny money than a Social Crediter could think up in an opium dream! Leather bills, playing card notes, silver dollars with holes in them, coins in halves and quarters.

I suppose the thing that made the article acceptable and salable was the silly little sneer about funny money and Social Credit-ers. I hope that was not the reason why the Toronto Star Weekly put the article in; there is no group of people in the world today that appreciates, advocates and understands sound money more than Social Crediters do. The money they propose is as far from funny money as it can possibly be. Further on he uses these words:
According to James E. Coyne, Donald Gordon's successor as deputy governor of the Bank of Canada, our money today has value because its quantity is limited. It's pretty obvious, says Mr. Coyne, that if the amount of money in circulation were infinitely increased, its value would decline to very near that of the paper it's printed on. He, therefore, defines it as one of the key functions of the bank to see that money remains reasonably scarce.
As if any poor lunatic had ever advocated "infinitely" increasing it. I suppose the article was rendered salable once more because of this reference to "infinitely" increasing it, as though anyone had ever advocated anything like that in Canada.

The resourceful Hudson's Bay Company solved the exchange problem by issuing its own copper tokens, based on a beaver skin as the standard of value. The largest coin represented one beaver pelt, a second one-half a beaver pelt and the smallest one-quarter of a beaver pelt. If Ojibway Indian Joe Hoot Owl brought in a beaver but wanted only a clay pipe from the company store, the company could give him three quarter-tokens change, good another day.
There is Canadian money. In this case the symbols were created beyond question. They did not have to borrow them from any bank. The article goes on:	*
But the governors of New France had no means of coining money, and it wasn't long before they were forced to improvise. And their innovation was a dandy. In 1685 the intendant, Jacques de Meulles, strapped for cash to pay his soldiers and staff, hit on the idea of paying them off with playing cards, which were abundant. He stamped them with the royal coat of arms, signed them, and paid them out at the rate of one card to a four-franc note. The cards were further cut up into halves and quarters for smaller amounts. These playing cards constituted one of the earliest forms of paper money in the western world.
There are the symbols again. They were made. Did they work? Of course they

I appreciate the kindness of the hon. member for Calgary West. I continue with the article:
De Meulles and succeeding intendants, fairly responsible men, tried to keep new currency on a sound footing. They would redeem the card money with gold and silver whenever France sent any, taking it back from the merchants when supplies of food, clothing and other commodities came from the old country.
But trouble began in 1690 when a cargo of flour and pork sank on the way out.
Goods, you see.
Similar cargoes went down in 1691 and 1692. The intendant had issued fresh card money against the arrival of these goods. The people and the merchants were stuck with cards, hut no goods, and a great outcry arose. This was perhaps Canada's first taste of inflation.
Altogether the author has done a pretty good job. He shows what caused-what always causes-inflation, namely, a shortage of goods in relation to the amount of money, not' the kind of money, what it was made of, or where it came from. I continue:
The financial structure of the country was undermined by experiences like this, as the French colonial regimes issued more and more unbacked notes during the 18th century struggle for supremacy with England. Only a fraction of the paper money outstanding was redeemed by the French government after the capitulation of Quebec in 1759. Not surprisingly, the whole institution of paper money suffered loss of prestige, and the long-memoried habitants stoutly resisted early attempts to establish banks of currency issue when the British took over.
It is only fair to put that in as part of the article. I continue:
It was through the imperial army, of all institutions, that confidence in paper money was re-established, and the way paved for the rush of private bank openings that featured the early part of the 19th century. To pay running charges of the war of 1812, bills were issued against the credit of Britain. These usually bore interest and, more important, they were redeemed within four or five years.
It does not say whether redeemed in goods. If they were, that was good enough. I continue:
Another distinct phase of Canadian monetary history, the issuance of private paper money, began about 30 years before the banks got into the business, and flourished for several decades. The acceptance of these notes depended on the firm's or individual's reputation. The Montreal antiquarian, P. N. Breton, listed 41 individuals and firms which issued paper money, including several breweries

The Address-Mr. Blackmore and several city corporations. A favourite denomination of the city notes was 7J pence.
Here is the last quotation I shall use:
To say that the world today is more complicated than it has ever been is to state a truism. But for Mr. Average Canadian, the vital matter of currency has achieved a simplicity and uniformity unequalled since the days when the red man ruled'.
That is just the trouble, Your Honour. The ordinary citizen thinks that everything is well with our money, whereas there never was a time when everything was much worse than it is with our money, because our money is simply not adequate to the task we must have it perform.
I should like to thank the Toronto Star Weekly for the article. It shows a desire to have the truth about money. If the Star Weekly will go forward and give the Canadian people the actual facts about money it will perform the greatest service it has ever performed in this country in all its long history.
What is sound money? What is a sound dollar? A dollar having constant buying power. I fancy hon. members will say, "I want a dollar which will buy the same amount of goods ten years from now as it will buy today." That is what everybody thinks about when he thinks about sound money. Our money is a long, long way from that.
I have here a set of figures which hon. members will be interested in. These figures were compiled for me by the finance department and submitted to me in a letter dated March 2,1950. They show the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar from 1927 down to 1949, inclusive. I am going to run down right through the list, so that when it is on Hansard members may read it tomorrow. We are taking the Canadian dollar of 1939 as 100. We are saying it is worth 100 cents. What was the 1939 Canadian dollar worth in 1927? What is that same 1939 dollar worth today? That is what we are asking ourselves, to see whether our Canadian dollar is sound. This table will set out the value of our dollar in the various years, taking the base of 100 for

And it is still going down. Will anyone say that is a sound dollar? Well, he will be courageous if he does, and he will have a hard job proving it.
What is a sound dollar? I submit that one definition of a sound dollar is one that does not fluctuate in value. Is a sound dollar money backed by gold? Is it money backed by securities and bonds? Is it money lent by the banks? Is it money backed by the credit of a person, a company or a community?
What is credit? It may be described in two sentences: First, the money-producing power of a country and, secondly, the goods-and-services producing power of the country.
Again, is it always money that is scarce that is sound, as was implied by Mr. Coyne's statement? Is it money that is adequately distributed, like blood? Money has been called the bloodstream of the state. But blood would not be much good to one's body if it did not reach his toes and his hair. Money is not really sound in a state if it cannot reach adequately every individual of the state. Money is the bloodstream of the state, remember!
Now, sound money is money with at least three characteristics: Firstly, it must have plenty of goods and services behind it and in front of it; and, secondly, have behind it or under it a price structure which is not fluctuating unduly; and, thirdly, must be adequately distributed. Anything short of that is not sound money.
There is a monetary problem in the world. "The Story of Money" by Sir Norman Angell, published in 1929, an excellent book, is a very careful study of the whole of the world's money. He closes his work with these words:
One thing at least, then, the survey has proved, that there is a monetary problem, and that the task of its solution deserves the efforts of our wisest economists and boldest statesmen.
That was in 1929, before the depression. Did he know what he was talking about? I submit he probably did.

People generally must come to understand money. The closing words of the introductory note in the same book, just before chapter one, are these:
Money can never be a safe and dependable device in a society made up of people who are ignorant of its nature. We are now facing a monetary revolution.
One sentence more I have left out, because it does not seem to have any bearing on what I am saying. Do you agree with that? Well, if we are facing a monetary revolution, what changes are you going to make? What is the matter? Why do we need a monetary revolution?
In Sir Norman Angell's fine little booklet "Your Money", published in 1936, comprising a series of articles which the Financial Post had Sir Norman Angell prepare in order to set Social Crediters right in 1935, we find the following words on page 1:
Without some knowledge upon which to base such decisions, democracy itself is impossible. To know what we are doing, what we are talking about when we discuss these matters, we must know something of the nature of money. Our whole civilization rests upon insecure foundations so long as most of us are completely ignorant of such a subject as this.
What an astonishing thing, Mr. Speaker, to find so little discussion of money in this house! And almost none in the responsible papers of the country-except that, of course, which seeks to discredit those who wish to discuss money! It seems to indicate that a change of attitude is needed.
I have discussed to some extent what sound money is. I should like now to read into the record a statement which I think is of very great value, and one which I have read before. This is a statement by the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, chairman of the Midland bank in England for many years. It occurs in his report to his shareholders in January of 1936, and is found in The Times, down in our library, for January 30 of that year. These are, I believe, words of great importance:
We learnt that a shortage of money may be just as vicious in its effects as an excess, though deflation has still a touch of virtue about it in the minds of many people. Nevertheless it is becoming more and more widely recognized that greater productivity calls for an increased supply of money, for otherwise prices will fall, business will stagnate, and the growing productive capacity will be unused.
For money to be truly "sound" there must be enough of it to finance an ordinarily growing volume of trade, yet not so much as to give rise to an inflationary movement of prices.
The whole secret of success in managing our monetary affairs is to build up a system under which we can be sure that there will be plenty of money when there is plenty of
The Address-Mr. Noseworthy goods. The last depression came on because we had plenty of goods and did not know how to get enough money into circulation.
What is enough money? Suppose we accept the statement of Mr. James E. Coyne, that we need a scarcity of money. Scarce in reference to what? Is it the number of people in the community? Is it the goods and services producing capacity of the community? Is it the goods and services actually available for consumption in that community, or the goods and exchanges to be made?
The answer is that it is the goods and exchanges which are to be made. May I quote from "Your Money", by Sir Norman Angell:
Having dealt in the previous article with the chief money illusion-which is broadly that money, even when it is the precious metals, is itself wealth and that a nation enriches itself by the simple fact of increasing its store of money-we deal in this chapter with what might be called the chief money truth. This truth is that when you do increase the quantity of a nation's money out of proportion to the quantity of goods or exchanges to -be made, you get a rise of prices; that when you decrease it, you get a fall.
Our whole problem is to devise a money system whereby we can avoid either an inappropriate increase or an inappropriate decrease of circulating money. I maintain that the only mechanism which has been suggested thus far for doing that very thing is to be found in the Social Credit proposals.

Mr. Speaker, I want to assure hon. members who are waiting for the vote that I shall be brief. I am constantly amazed when listening to the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) and caused to wonder why it is that ministers of finance the world over should have to struggle as they do when there is such an easy means at their disposal as outlined by members of the Social Credit group. It is amazing to me that the men in charge of finance in the different nations should not be ready to accept a plan that could be carried out with such great ease.
I rise to support the subamendment. The subamendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) does not ask us to subscribe to a social credit method of carrying out the principles involved therein. I support it because more than 2,000 people in the riding I represent have written to me within the past few weeks protesting against the means test as applied to old age pensions. I support it because I am confident that these people do not want to have to wait for the removal of the means test until we have established and built up in this country a contributory old age pension scheme.

The Address-Mr. Noseworthy
As has been pointed out, the government committed itself in 1945 to exactly the kind of old age pension provided for in the subamendment, and I quote from page 37 of the green book as follows:
As part of the general proposals now put before the conference, it is proposed that the federal government would establish a system of national old age pensions entirely financed and administered by the federal government, and paid at the uniform rate of $30 per month regardless of means to men and women aged 70 and over in all parts of Canada.
I submit that that is the type of old age pension plan to which this government was committed in 1945, to which it committed itself in the election of 1949 and from which it is trying to get away at the present time. While I am on my feet I should like to read a few quotations from a petition which I presume every hon. member has received from the old age pensioners' society of Manitoba. Speaking of the means test it says:
We regard the means test as one of the most iniquitous pieces of legislation that could be enacted in any country against its citizens.
I would remind the Liberal members of the house that those are almost exactly the words used by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) in his election campaign speeches in June 1949. They go on to say:
We despise and reject any attempt to bring about communism in this land, but we also insist that causes or laws which create a feeling of inequality, dissatisfaction and suffering should be removed at the earliest possible moment.
1.	We, as a body, desire freedom and encouragement to proceed with any kind of labour, for which each individual has been fitted.
2.	To be allowed and assisted to sell the product of our hands or minds just as freely as any other citizen of our country, whether on the old age pension or off it.
3.	To accept jobs or occupations whenever and wherever offered, with the opportunity of being paid for the product of our hands or minds without in any way affecting our pension.
A party that is crying for free enterprise, a party that insists it is maintaining freedom in this country, should be ready to accept this proposal and give to old age pensioners the same type of freedom that they insist should be given to other citizens. The petition continues:
We object to any form of slavery such as the means test imposes (1) when we are denied the privilege of accepting a gift from a relative or friend, without being penalized for it, or being deprived of part or all of our pension.
5. We object to being disallowed to earn anything above the $50 a month limit set without penalty.
The restrictions on the old age pensioners means, frequently, being shut up in a little room, living on one or two meals a day, with no social or congenial surroundings, and not able to attend meetings for mutual satisfaction, because they cannot walk the distances required to do so; and with the meagre pension allowance, increase in rents, cost of living increases, transportation charges, et cetera, they cannot use any means of conveyance.

We are not unmindful of the fact that certain Canadian officials are being paid huge salaries of $25,000 per annum with a pension allowance, not of $40 a month but of $6,000 a year, while others receive a salary of $20,000 a year and receive a pension of $5,000 a year.
That reference to pensions reminds me of a newspaper article dated January 14 which contained an account of the retirement of the manager of the American Telephone and Telegraph Company. This man had been receiving a salary of $209,000 and he was pensioned on January 1, 1950, with a pension of $95,000 a year. I bring that in because of another question raised by my constituents and about which I have received many letters. I refer to the lack of service being given by the Canadian subsidiary of this parent company which can afford to retire its manager on a pension of $95,000 a year. I refer to the Bell Telephone Company of Canada.
In the Toronto area alone today there are close to 12,000 home owners who, although they live in communities that have every other convenience, have applied for telephones but cannot get them although they may be needed in case of sickness or for other reasons. I want to take advantage of this opportunity to call to the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), under whose department the affairs of that company come, the fact that we have a situation where a utility serving the public, and which is now asking for an increase in its rates after just having floated a new debenture loan, according to its own report has today across Canada approximately 200,000 applications for new telephones and improved telephone services. I think as members of the house we have some responsibility for a company which is rendering as important a public service as the Bell Telephone Company. In addition to registering my protest against the government for failing at' this session to remove the means test from old age pensions, I also want to register my protest against the kind of service we are getting from the Bell Telephone Company in the Toronto area.

speechtext: What efforts are being made by the Department of National Health and Welfare to control, alleviate or eliminate the occupational disabilities that develop among professional civil pilots?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: OCCUPATIONAL
speechtext:
The most common occupational disabilities that develop among professional civil pilots are:
(1)	Damage to the hearing mechanism caused by the vibration and noise of aircraft and radio navigation aids, and
(2)	Flying fatigue.
Regarding (1), the Department of National Health and Welfare is making a complete survey and study of all causes and effects of hearing damage among civil pilots. This is aimed at establishing ways and means of early recognition of such damage and will establish the patterns whereby civil pilots and the Department of Transport will be advised of necessary control measures.
Regarding (2), this problem has been under study by the Department of National Health and Welfare for some months. Following the completion of this study the department will suggest appropriate hours of flight duty and rest periods for civil pilots, within limits that are economically sound and still consistent with maximum flight safety.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
These questions are somewhat similar in substance to questions asked by the same hon. member on the first of March to which I gave the answer that is reported at page 352 of Hansard. In form, and especially in the French translation, the question is quite objectionable. In the French translation it reads:
De qui releve, qui effectue ou a qui est confiee la distribution des faveurs ministerielles, pour le compte du gouvernement federal...
The English translation of the French is "the distribution of ministerial favours for the account of the federal government." There are no ministerial favours and nothing which could be translated as "ministerial favours" if that is what is meant by patronage. The question in English reads:
Who administers, handles, or has charge of, the patronage on behalf of the federal government . . .
No one has charge of patronage on behalf of the federal government. It may be that certain members or persons make recommendations to ministers about appointments or other matters in connection with the public service, but no one handles or administers patronage for the federal government. The only knowledge I have of anything of that kind is that one of the defeated candidates in a by-election asked me who was going to handle patronage. I told him that to my knowledge there was no patronage, that there were persons who made certain recommendations to which more or less importance was attached, but that was all there was to it. I think this is the kind of partisan political warfare which should not be spread upon the orders of the day.

Reference has been made to standing order 50. That reference appears in Hansard for March 10 at page 672. Standing order 50, found at page 129 of Beauchesne's third edition, reads:
A motion to refer a bill, resolution or any question to the committee of the whole or any standing or special committee shall preclude all amendment of the main question.
I think it is fair to say that this standing order has been cited in debates on points of order a number of times, and it does create confusion in the minds of some hon. members. It seems to me, however, that if we take a moment to analyse the standing order its wording is clear, and the logic of it is also quite clear. Standing order 50 says in effect that if there is before the house a proposition that I will call A, whether it is a resolution, a bill or a question, and then some hon. member moves what I shall call B, namely a motion to refer A to the committee of the whole or to some standing or special committee, then it is not in order for someone else to try to get around B over to A. In other words as long as there is a motion before the house to refer the earlier question-the question of substance-to a committee, it is not in order to try to get around that motion of reference to amend the terms of the main motion.
I point out, however, that what we have before the house in the motion of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) is not a motion to refer anything at all. It is a motion for the appointment of a committee, a substantive motion in itself. It so happens that the word "refer" does not
Old Age Security
even appear in the motion. Indeed, as yet there is no committee to which this subject could be referred. So I repeat that what is before us is a motion to appoint a committee.
Then I ask Your Honour to take note of standing order 38, found at pages 87 and 88 of Beauchesne's, third edition. It is lengthy and I shall not read it all, but please note:
The following motions are debatable:	Every
motion-
Then follow a series lettered from (a) to (m), and included therein is:
(j) for the appointment of a committee.
There we have clearly stated a rule which applies to the motion before the house. It says that motions such as this one are debatable. Then if Your Honour will note subsection (2) of standing order 38, it says:
(2) All other motions, including adjournment motions, shall be decided without debate or amendment.
Surely it is clear from subsection (2) of standing order 38, which says that other motions shall be decided without debate or amendment, that the motions referred to in subsection (1) paragraphs (a) to (m) are subject to both debate and amendment. In other words I submit it is quite clear that the kind of motion we now have before us, that is a motion for the appointment of a committee, is subject to both debate and amendment; and it is under that right to amend the motion that I claim my right to move my amendment, and also because of that right I submit that standing order 50 does not apply to a motion of this kind.
The Acting Speaker on March 10 also asked us to note certain instances in Hansard of bygone years, and in the Journals. I have looked up the two references he gave us at that time. The first was to page 2588 of Hansard for May 17, 1929, which relates to a motion for Mr. Speaker to leave the chair for the house to go into committee of the whole on a certain proposed money resolution. The leader of the opposition of that day sought to amend the terms of the resolution; and Mr. Speaker, I think correctly, applied standing order 50.

It can examine and study possible alternative measures of old age security for Canada, with or without a means test for beneficiaries, including plans based on contributory insurance principles. I do not need to refer to the rest of the motion, as it does not relate to the point. There is the crux of the matter, and the crux of the crux, if I may say so, is the word "alternative". This motion gives the committee the right to study possible alternative measures. I am satisfied that if I were a member of that committee, and I moved that we study the possibility of recommending, not an alternative measure,

but the removal of the means test from the present old age pension, I would be told by the chairman that that went beyond the terms of reference.
It is to make it absolutely clear that we have the right to discuss the proposal I make that I feel my amendment should be placed before the house. I wish to thank hon. members for the assistance which they have given to me.

During Friday's debate on the motion of the Minister of National Health and Welfare to appoint a joint committee on old age security, a proposed amendment was moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and a proposed subamendment by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell). During the course of the debate the deputy chairman of committees, who was then in the Speaker's chair, issued a caveat concerning the admissibility of the proposed amendment and subamendment.
I have listened with interest to the very able and cogent arguments which have been advanced to the effect that standing order 50 is not applicable and it may be that on another occasion serious consideration may have to be given to these representations. There are, however, other precedents which must be considered at this time. For instance Bourinot, in his Parliamentary Procedure, fourth edition, at page 316, states clearly that:
The object of an amendment is to effect some alteration in a question . . .
Proposed amendments which neither add to nor subtract from the main motion have been held to be inadmissible. (See Canadian Commons Journals, 1948, volume 74, page 229, and House of Commons Debates for March 8, 1948, at page 1993, and Beauchesne's third edition, citation 407.)
The main motion, in this instance, empowers the proposed joint committee to examine and study "possible alternative measures of old age security for Canada, with or without a means test for beneficiaries, including plans based on contributory insurance principles." The proposed amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would insert immediately thereafter the following words:
. . . and also the possibility of the immediate removal of the means test from the present old age pension;
It seems clear that the words "possible alternative measures of old age security for Canada" are sufficiently broad to cover the removal of the means test from the present old age pension. It seems equally clear that the concluding words:
. . . with or without a means test for beneficiaries, including plans based on contributory insurance principles,
were not intended to, and do not in fact, limit in any way the generality of the immediately preceding words. This being so, I must conclude that the proposed amendment adds nothing to and subtracts nothing from the main motion. Since the proposed amendment is otiose, I must rule that it is out of order. Moreover, even if the proposed amendment would, in fact, have conferred wider powers
Old Age Security
on the committee, it would in my view have run counter to citation 546 of Beauchesne's third edition, which reads as follows:
When the house is considering a motion, of which notice has been given, for the appointment of a select committee, a member cannot move an amendment that the committee be given wider powers than those which were set down in the notice.
I believe that citation applies particularly to the subamendment which was moved by the hon. member for Macleod.
It reads as follows:
That the following words be added to the end of the first paragraph, "and to examine the possibility of granting pensions to incurables who are unable to earn a livelihood."
The amendment being out of order, the proposed subamendment is of course also out of order. However, while it is not necessary for me to do so, I should perhaps add that, in any event, it does not purport to amend the amendment, and therefore it would be inadmissible as a subamendment. (See Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, citation 364.) Moreover, even if moved as an amendment, it would in my view be out of order under citation 546 of Beauchesne's third edition.
